entry.title: Marcus Aurelius Was the First SRE (And His Meditations Is the Best Production Run book Ever Written)
entry.summary: Hear me out. Reading his Meditations recently, I kept noticing the same structure repeating Every core Stoic principle maps directly to modern production engineering: Premeditatio malorum → Chaos engineering Dichotomy of Control → Blast radius scoping Memento mori → Documentation culture Obstacle is the Way → Incident-driven improvement The Bhagavad Gita — another ancient text — describes three fundamental states of consciousness called the Gunas. They map perfectly to code quality: Sattva → Pure functions. Clean output. Low cognitive overhead. Exits with code 0. ✅ Rajas → High activity, high anxiety. Output dependent on ego. Unresolved promises. ⚠️ Tamas → Deadlocked processes. Technical debt hoarding. System sleeping at peak load. Never exits. ❌ Which Guna is your current sprint running in? We spend billions on productivity tools, methodologies, and frameworks. The Stoics solved most of these problems 2,000 years ago with nothing but a wax tablet and radical commitment to systems thinking. Marcus Aurelius wasn't a philosopher writing for posterity. He was an engineer debugging his own operating system — in real time, under maximum load, with no safety net. That's the most relatable thing I've ever read. I've been building interactive versions of these ancient texts as developer frameworks — decision trees, SLO mappings, post-mortem templates. If you're curious what that looks like: → Quantum Manuals on Selar Creative interpretation of classical philosophy for modern builders. Not academic—executable._**

entry.title: Understanding Word2Vec – Part 2: Converting Words into Neural Network Inputs
entry.summary:
In the previous article, we just got started with the concept Word2Vec and assigning numbers to words. We will now see how to represent it in the form of a neural network. To show how we can get a neural network to figure out what numbers should go with different words, let’s imagine we have two phrases: The Incredibles is great! Despicable Me is great! To create a neural network that figures out what numbers we should associate with each word, the first thing we do is create inputs for each unique word. For simplicity, assume the movie name is treated as a single word. In this case, we have 4 unique words in the training data, so we create 4 input nodes.
Next, each input is connected to at least one activation function.
These activation functions use the identity function, which means the input value is exactly the same as the output value. The number of activation functions corresponds to how many numbers we want to associate with each word. The weights on these connections are the actual numbers we associate with each word. In this example, we want to associate two numbers with each word.
These weights initially start with random values. During training, they are optimized using backpropagation, which we will explore in the next article.
